corrected_proposal.title: Federal Court Blocks Trump's Order Targeting the Minority Business Agency
corrected_proposal.description_short: EO 14238 directed MBDA to sharply reduce functions; a federal court later preliminarily enjoined implementation after staff and grant actions.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Trump signed Executive Order 14238 on March 14, 2025, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions and reduce statutory operations and staffing to the legal minimum. The Rhode Island federal court later recorded that most MBDA staff were placed on leave and grants appeared terminated, then granted a preliminary injunction. This account corrects the February date and does not claim all federal minority-business support ended.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 14, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14238, directing the Minority Business Development Agency to eliminate nonstatutory functions to the maximum extent allowed by law and reduce statutory work and staffing to the legal minimum. Afterward, MBDA placed all but five employees on paid administrative leave, and the district court said the agency appeared to have terminated its existing grants. In its May 6 preliminary order, the U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island stated that the executive order, as carried out, violated the Administrative Procedure Act in an arbitrary and capricious way and disregarded Congress’s role in authorizing agencies and appropriating funds. The court granted a preliminary injunction against implementing the order at MBDA. That was a preliminary ruling, not a final merits judgment. The records do not show that all federal minority-business support or SBA programs ended, or establish later agency operations after the injunction.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Rhode Island

corrected_proposal.description_short: DOJ withdrew eight OVW grant notices in February 2025, then issued revised opportunities in May. The record documents a pause and reissue, not elimination of all OVW grants.

corrected_proposal.description_long: On February 6, 2025, the Justice Department’s Office on Violence Against Women removed eight grant opportunities from its website and said the notices were under revision. The 19th reported that no updated notices appeared until May 7, after the original application deadlines. Three months after the withdrawal, six new opportunities were posted; only two matched the original set. On May 23, DOJ announced 19 fiscal year 2025 funding notices for programs addressing domestic and dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. The reported pause and later release show that grant opportunities were withdrawn, delayed, and reissued with revised terms. They do not establish that DOJ eliminated every OVW grant, terminated more than $500 million in annual funding, or ended survivor services nationwide. The available sources do not document shelters turning people away or deaths caused by the pause. The May funding announcement also shows other OVW opportunities remained available.

corrected_proposal.title: House Republicans Proposed Tightening Universal School-Meal Eligibility
corrected_proposal.description_short: A March 2025 House Republican budget proposal would raise the school-meal CEP threshold from 25% to 60%.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: Chalkbeat reported that a House Republican budget proposal would raise the Community Eligibility Provision threshold from 25% to 60%. An advocacy-group estimate cited in the report projected that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected. The story describes a proposal, not an enacted March rollback.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On March 12, 2025, Chalkbeat reported that House Republicans were considering a budget proposal to raise the Community Eligibility Provision’s minimum identified-student percentage from 25 percent to 60 percent. The provision lets qualifying schools serve meals at no charge to all enrolled students. The 25 percent threshold came from USDA’s 2023 final rule. Chalkbeat cited an advocacy group’s estimate that more than 24,000 schools and about 12 million students could be affected if the threshold changed. Those figures described projected exposure under a proposal, not a count of students who lost meals. The report did not describe an enacted USDA rollback or an immediate removal of free meals. The proposal concerned a potential eligibility change; the available sources do not establish that it became law or that schools stopped serving meals because of it. Schools below the proposed threshold could lose eligibility if the change were enacted.

source_fact_map.fact: Chalkbeat reported the House Republican proposal would raise the CEP threshold from 25 percent to 60 percent and attributed the projected school/student impact to an advocacy organization.
source_fact_map.quote: The House Republican proposal would raise the share to 60% — higher than the threshold has ever been. That would kick more than 24,000 schools off of community eligibility, and some 12 million students would no longer automatically qualify for free meals, Hysom’s organization estimated.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: One proposal would dramatically increase the share of students who need to be enrolled in aid programs — such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families — for schools to be eligible to serve free meals to all kids through the Community Eligibility Provision. Right now, schools need to show 25% of students are enrolled in those kinds of assistance programs to participate in community eligibility. The House Republican proposal would raise the share to 60% — higher than the threshold has ever been. That would kick more than 24,000 schools off of community eligibility, and some 12 million students would no longer automatically qualify for free meals, Hysom’s organization estimated.

corrected_proposal.title: USDA’s July 2025 PRWORA Notice Includes WIC, With State Implementation Varying
corrected_proposal.description_short: USDA’s July 10 notice listed WIC among food programs treated as federal public benefits; it did not announce the frozen record’s claimed February nationwide ban.
corrected_proposal.description_medium: On July 10, 2025, USDA published a notice interpreting PRWORA’s federal-public-benefit definition and listing WIC among the Food and Nutrition Service’s programs. USDA said it was still evaluating how to verify compliance and would issue later guidance. The notice supports a July agency interpretation, not a February blanket exclusion of lawful immigrant families. A contemporaneous NILC analysis said states could choose whether to offer or restrict WIC; it reported Idaho was the only state restricting federally funded WIC that month.
corrected_proposal.description_long: On July 10, 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture published a notice interpreting how the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act applies to the programs it administers. The notice included the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) among Food and Nutrition Service programs meeting the statute’s federal-public-benefit definition. USDA said it was still evaluating how to verify compliance and planned to issue later guidance. A contemporaneous National Immigration Law Center analysis said states could choose whether to offer or restrict WIC; it reported that Idaho alone had restricted federally funded WIC by July 2025. The notice documents a July federal interpretation, not a February nationwide ban on lawful immigrant families.
